articles.title: How ICE Operates in the Shadows
articles.author: Aala Abdullahi
articles.summary: The black vehicles with tinted windows converged on the bus stop just after 5:30 a.m. It was June 18, 2025, and Pedro Vasquez Perdomo and his co-workers were drinking coffee, waiting for a ride to a construction job in Pasadena, California. Masked, armed men poured from the vehicles and charged at them. Vasquez Perdomo thought they were probably immigration agents, but he couldn’t be sure. The agents wore plain clothes with no visible badges and didn’t identify themselves. They seized the 54-year-old Vasquez Perdomo, handcuffed him, chained his feet, waist and hands, and hauled him away. No one showed him a warrant or told him why they were arresting him, he later wrote in a declaration . “It felt like a kidnapping,” he wrote. The agents drove Vasquez Perdomo and his coworkers to B-18, an immigration processing site in the basement of a federal building in downtown Los Angeles. Some lawyers had dubbed the facility a “black hole,” because detainees could be hard to locate or reach there. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to requests for comment for this story. Attorneys often can’t figure out where ICE is detaining people—and can’t see the evidence against them.

articles.summary: If Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is the business world’s Bugs Bunny, playing every position on the baseball field by himself, Elon Musk is its Forrest Gump, materializing at the center of events both strange and consequential. In just the past 10 days, Musk has cut a $1 billion check to help the Ellisons build a right-leaning media empire; tested market jitters with a gargantuan SpaceX bond offering ; set in motion the largest-ever corporate merger and the largest-ever philanthropic gift ; and set a new standard for all corporate demo days with an actual flying car . Further from Wall Street, he reset US foreign policy by cutting Ukraine off from Starlink — a move that says enough about who’s in charge that President Donald Trump claimed credit for reversing it — and dominated the midterm-elections homestretch with spending that will near $450 million this cycle. After his post-DOGE meltdown last year, many had thought Musk had been neutered. He lost his lawsuit against OpenAI. SpaceX’s grandiose IPO prospectus drew titters from an investment community generally prone to believe outlandish promises. But like X, Musk has emerged stronger and more central to finance, politics, and culture.

articles.author: Rose Horowitch
articles.summary: Updated at 2:27 p.m. ET on October 26, 2026 N othing makes me more nauseated than a row of multiple-choice questions and empty bubbles. After I turned 18, I thought I’d never encounter that feeling again, outside of stress dreams about forgetting my No. 2 pencils. And yet there I was, hiding in a cubicle at work to take a test intended for high schoolers, demonstrating my understanding of apostrophe placement and verb tense, and comparing the definition of truth in passages from Nietzsche and JFK. I was taking the Classic Learning Test, an alternative to the SAT and ACT. The test is only 11 years old, and was originally taken mainly by kids who were homeschooled or had attended private religious academies.
